Haida sacred narratives center on the Raven (Xhuuya/Nankil'slas), the culture hero and transformer who shaped the world and freed the sun and the tides; the wolf appears chiefly as a crest and clan emblem carved on poles, never as a worshipped god. The water-spirit archetype is a template artifact.

research_notes: Tribe: Haida. The record's 'water-spirit / guardian of the deserts' fields are template filler with no basis. Raven (Xhuuya/Nankil'slas) is the Haida culture hero and transformer; the wolf is a crest and clan figure, not an object of worship. No wolf deity is attested in Haida ethnography or the native-languages.org Haida corpus.

description: Not independently attested as a wolf deity among the Kwakwaka'wakw. Their central creative and trickster figure is Raven, who made the islands, released daylight, and shaped the first humans from wood and clay; the wolf is a respected hereditary crest figure, not an object of worship. The water-spirit framing is a template artifact.
source: Wikipedia, Kwakwaka'wakw mythology; no wolf deity attested in ethnographic sources
research_notes: Tribe: Kwakwaka'wakw (older spelling Kwakiutl). Raven is the creator-trickster; the wolf is a hereditary crest and founding ancestor of chiefly lines (e.g., the Dzawada'enuxw wolf origin), not a deity. 'Guardian of the valleys' and the water-spirit archetype are template junk.

description: Not independently attested as a wolf deity in Yurok folklore. Yurok tradition is carried by the trickster-heroes Pulekukwerek and Wohpekumeu, recorded by Kroeber, Sapir, and Spott and Kroeber, who put the world in order and bestow power on worthy humans. The wolf is a familiar animal of the Klamath watershed, not a worshipped deity.
source: Kroeber 1911; Sapir 1928; Spott & Kroeber 1942; no Yurok wolf deity attested
research_notes: Tribe: Yurok. The culture heroes Pulekukwerek and Wohpekumeu carry Yurok cosmology in the recorded corpora (Kroeber 1911, Sapir 1928, Spott & Kroeber 1942). No wolf deity is attested; 'guardian of the swamps' is template filler.

description: Not independently attested as a wolf ghost in Choctaw folklore. The attested Choctaw spirit beings include Nalusa Falaya, a shadowy figure who slips along trails to attack travelers, and the little forest people Bohpoli and Kowi Anukasha; no wolf specter or wolf ghost appears in the recorded corpus documented by Swanton.
source: Swanton, Choctaw mythology; Native-Languages.org; no wolf ghost attested
research_notes: Tribe: Choctaw. Attested spirits are Nalusa Falaya (shadowy night being), Bohpoli/Kowi Anukasha (little people), and Kashehotapalo; none is a wolf ghost. The 'ghost' type and 'guardian of the rivers' field are template-generated.

description: Not independently attested as a wolf ghost in Hopi tradition. The Hopi katsinam include Kweo, a wolf kachina who is a great hunter and pathfinder guiding villages to game, and wolves appear in the world-age account of the second world; a malevolent wolf specter is not part of the ceremonial record.
source: Smithsonian NMAI, Kweo wolf kachina records; Hopi village records; no wolf ghost attested
research_notes: Tribe: Hopi. The wolf is represented as the Kweo wolf kachina, a beneficent hunter-teacher and pathfinder (Smithsonian NMAI), and appears in the second-world age account; no wolf ghost exists. The 'ghost' type is template-generated.

description: No standalone wolf guardian spirit is attested in Cheyenne folklore; the record inflates a real tradition. The wolf's central Cheyenne presence is the Wolf Warriors, a renowned military society honoring the wolf's wariness and skill, and wolves appear in tales as helpers and teachers. The animal is honored for endurance, not worshipped as a nature-spirit deity.
source: Cheyenne Wolf Warrior (Konianutqio) society, Plains ethnography; no wolf guardian deity attested
research_notes: Tribe: Cheyenne. Wolves appear in tales as helpers and teachers and as namesake of the Wolf Warriors (Konianutqio), a genuine military society. No wolf guardian deity is attested; the description is reframed to the real wolf-centered tradition.

Yurok cosmology is carried by the culture heroes Pulekukwerek and Wohpekumeu, who established customs, dances, and the balance of the world as told by Kroeber, Sapir, and Spott and Kroeber; no wolf guardian figure appears in their recorded stories.

research_notes: Tribe: Yurok. No wolf guardian figure exists; Yurok power beings are the trickster-heroes and the wealth spirits of the Klamath. 'Guardian of the oceans' is template filler. Unattested.

description: Not independently attested as a wolf nature-spirit deity among the Blackfoot. Wolves appear as powerful helpers in Blackfoot tales, most famously in the Wolf Man story, where a pack saves a husband from his murderous wives; wolves are respected allies, but no wolf spirit-deity of nature is recorded.
source: The Wolf Man Blackfoot legend; Native-Languages.org; no wolf nature-spirit deity attested
research_notes: Tribe: Blackfoot (USA). Wolves are helper-figures; the Wolf Man story (a man saved from murderous wives by a pack) is genuine Blackfoot lore. No nature-spirit wolf deity is attested. Duplicate of the Canada record.

description: The wolf is a foundational crest figure of the Haida, one of the principal clan emblems along with the Raven, Eagle, and Killer Whale, carved on poles and house fronts. In the legend of Wolf and the Sea, wolves pursue a sea creature underwater and are transformed, giving origin to the killer whales. No separate wolf deity is attested.
source: Native-Languages.org, Haida legends (Wolf and the Sea); Haida clan crest records
research_notes: Tribe: Haida. Wolf is one of the principal Haida clans/crests; the legend 'Wolf and the Sea' accounts for the origin of killer whales. Reframed from 'nature-spirit deity' to the attested crest-and-legend tradition; the wolf is not a standalone deity.

description: The wolf appears in Hopi kachina religion as Kweo, the wolf kachina, a great hunter, teacher, and pathfinder who helps villages find game and guides hunts. Wolves also figure in the Hopi account of the second world, when the ancestors took the forms of wolves and bears during their migrations. Kweo is a beneficent kachina, not an abstract nature-spirit deity.
source: Smithsonian NMAI, Kweo wolf kachina; Native-Languages.org/hopi-legends.htm; Pritzker 2000
research_notes: Tribe: Hopi. Kweo, the wolf kachina, is attested as a great hunter and pathfinder (Smithsonian NMAI); wolves also appear in the second-world age account (Pritzker). Honest reframe to the kachina tradition.

description: The wolf is a major hereditary crest of the Kwakwaka'wakw. The Dzawada'enuxw recall that their ancestors were four wolves who swam from the mainland and took human form, making the wolf a tutelary ancestor rather than an abstract nature-spirit. Wolves are honored in the winter ceremonial and as clan founders, not worshipped as separate nature spirits.
source: Dzawada'enuxw wolf-ancestor tradition; Kwakwaka'wakw crest records; Boas ethnographic collections
research_notes: Tribe: Kwakwaka'wakw. Wolf is a major crest; the Dzawada'enuxw trace descent from four wolves who took human form. Reframed as crest and tutelary ancestor rather than a nature-spirit deity.

description: Not independently attested as a wolf nature-spirit in Miwok folklore. Miwok creation is carried by Silver Fox, who sang the world into being, and Coyote, the ancestor of the people; the wolf plays no creator or spirit role in the recorded Miwok corpus. The record is a template-generated spirit with no tribal basis.
source: Miwok creation accounts (Silver Fox and Coyote); no wolf spirit attested in the Miwok corpus
research_notes: Tribe: Miwok. Creation belongs to Silver Fox and Coyote (O-let'-te, the ancestor), not the wolf. No wolf nature-spirit appears in the recorded Miwok corpus. 'Guardian of the cliffs' is template filler.

description: Wolf is a creator and culture hero in Paiute tradition, called Isa, who usually appears in human form and made the world and its people in the beginning; Coyote, his younger brother, follows him and brings folly, death, and change. Wolf is the elder and wiser of the pair, respected as the one who set the world in order.
source: Native-Languages.org, Paiute legends; Isa the Wolf as creator and culture hero
research_notes: Tribe: Paiute. Wolf (Isa) is a creator and culture hero, elder brother of Coyote, usually in man form but sometimes a literal wolf; attested at native-languages.org/paiute-legends.htm. Coyote is the younger trickster brother.

description: Not independently attested as a wolf trickster in Cheyenne folklore. The Cheyenne trickster is Veeho, a spider who takes human form and is both transformer-hero and fool; his name, often misread as 'White Man,' actually means 'Spider.' Cheyenne wolves instead belong to the Wolf Warrior society, an honored order, not trickster tales.
source: Native-Languages.org, Veeho the spider; no Cheyenne wolf trickster attested
research_notes: Tribe: Cheyenne. The trickster is Veeho (also Veho, Wihio), a spider in man form whose name means 'Spider,' not 'White Man'; he is transformer-hero in some tales and fool in most. Wolf belongs to the Wolf Warrior society, not trickster tales.

description: Amaguq is a wolf trickster-spirit in Inuit tradition, able to shape-shift between human and wolf form and known for clever, wily behavior in tales; the name is an Iñupiaq word for the wolf. He is distinct from Amarok, the lone giant wolf-spirit that preys on foolish hunters abroad at night.
source: Wikipedia, Inuit mythology (Amaguq); Byghan 2020; Snodgrass 1998
research_notes: Attested: Amaguq, a wolf trickster-spirit and shape-shifter, from the Iñupiaq word for wolf (Wikipedia; Byghan 2020; Snodgrass 1998). Distinct from Amarok, the lone giant wolf-spirit that hunts night hunters. 'Guardian of the deserts' is template filler.

Waters are instead the domain of figures such as Sedna of the sea; no wolf spirit is tied to rivers.

Coastal Northwest Coast traditions do include sea-connected women, such as the Haida Ocean Woman of recent retellings and Property Woman, who grants wealth, but no named 'Woman of the Sea' spirit appears in the ethnographic record. The entry is vague and unattested.

description: Not independently attested as a 'Wooden Person' spirit in Haida folklore. In related Kwakwaka'wakw tradition, Raven fashions the first man and woman from wood and clay, and Haida Raven likewise fashions people; these are episodes within Raven's creation work, not a distinct spirit. The record appears to distill that motif without a tribal basis.
source: Kwakwaka'wakw and Haida Raven creation accounts; no 'Wooden Person' spirit attested

description: White Bead Maiden (Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́), the young form of Changing Woman, was sought in marriage by the Sun, who came disguised as a handsome warrior. After many trials she traveled to his celestial house of turquoise and white shell, where she bore the Hero Twins, then returned to earth and became Changing Woman, the central female deity who governs the cycles of life and the seasons.
source: Navajo (Diné) oral tradition; ethnographies of Navajo religion; input appearance verified
research_notes: Tribe: Navajo (Diné). Yoołgaii Asdzą́ą́ is the youthful form of Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé), sought by the Sun; she bore the Hero Twins at his celestial house and later became Changing Woman. The input's appearance text is accurate and was lightly edited.

description: Xastc'inilgaiyîn, the White God of the East, is one of the directional Hactcin beings of the Jicarilla Apache. In the emergence story he holds the sun in the east and lets it travel across the sky, and with the other Hactcin he raised the great mountain and made reeds grow to build the ladder by which the people climbed into this world.
source: Jicarilla Apache emergence account (Goddard 1911; Opler); input appearance verified
research_notes: Tribe: Jicarilla Apache. Xastc'inilgaiyîn (White Hactcin) is one of the directional Hactcin; he is associated with the east and the sun, and the Hactcin raised the mountain and reed ladder of the emergence. The input's appearance text matches the emergence account.

description: Whirlwind, also rendered Cyclone, is the wind-being of the Jicarilla Apache creation, present before the world began alongside darkness and water. He is one of the primordial forces out of which the cosmos was ordered by the Hactcin, and he remains a power felt in the Southwest winds. The figure is attested in the Jicarilla emergence account.
source: Jicarilla Apache creation account (Goddard 1911; Opler 1938)
research_notes: Tribe: Jicarilla Apache. Cyclone (the whirlwind) is a primordial wind-being of the Jicarilla creation, alongside darkness and water. The input's appearance text was a copy-paste error from the White God of the East record and was replaced with the genuine figure. Possible duplicate of 'cyclone-apache' listed in related.

description: Not independently attested as 'Wise One' in the standard Apache ethnographic corpus. The Apache monster-slayer is Killer-of-Enemies, with Child of the Water in related traditions; the paired-brothers framing echoes Navajo heroic twins rather than any documented Apache 'Wise One.' The record appears to be a template construct without a firm source.
source: Opler, Goddard, Hoijer Apache collections; no 'Wise One' attested by that name
research_notes: Tribe: Apache (unspecified). No 'Wise One' is attested by that name in the standard corpus (Opler, Goddard, Hoijer). The Apache culture hero is Killer-of-Enemies (Child of the Water in related traditions); the younger-brother framing in the summary follows Navajo heroic twins. Unattested.

description: In the Cherokee story of how fire came to the people, Water Spider (Dilsdohdi, Kanane'ski Amai'yehi) volunteered when raven, hawk, and the other animals failed. She spun a bowl-shaped web, carried a burning coal across the water on her back, and brought fire to the world; her reddish mark recalls the ember she bore. Recorded by James Mooney.
source: Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee; Native-Languages.org; Cherokee spiritual beliefs
research_notes: Tribe: Cherokee. The fire-bringing spider is Dilsdohdi (Water Spider), who crossed the water with an ember in a web-bowl (Mooney). Note: the alias Dâyuni'sï is actually the water beetle of the Cherokee creation account, a different being; the confusion is flagged in the record and corrected in the description.

Lao animism centers on phi, or place and nature spirits, with no documented bear deity of the kind described; the white-furred moon-bear appears to be fabricated.

research_notes: Mis-attributed: a Laotian animist concept filed under USA with a Native American citation. Unattested in North American folklore.

description: Wokómásauwuu, Big Skeleton, is a Hopi spirit related to Masauwu, the Skeleton Man and deity of death and the earth's surface. In the story of the Ahö'li Kachina, Big Skeleton meets the kachinas and tells them to make their homes atop the mesas. He is a powerful being to be acknowledged and respected in Hopi ceremonial narratives.
source: Fewkes, Hopi Katcinas; Hopi village records; Wikipedia, Hopi mythology
research_notes: Tribe: Hopi. Wokómásauwuu relates to Masauwu (Skeleton Man, spirit of death); in the Ahö'li Kachina story he directs the kachinas to live atop the mesa (Fewkes, Hopi Katcinas). The input's appearance text is accurate.

description: Bull Snake is a character in the Hopi tale of Coyote and Bull Snake exchanging visits, recorded in the Traditions of the Hopi. Coyote finds Bull Snake's burrow beautiful and comfortable; the pair's exchange frames a homely lesson about envy and contentment. He is a narrative figure of a folktale, not a ceremonial spirit.
source: Voth, Traditions of the Hopi; two-friends Coyote and Bull Snake tale
research_notes: Tribe: Hopi. Bull Snake is a character in the folktale 'Two Friends: Coyote and Bull Snake Exchange Visits' (Voth, Traditions of the Hopi), which the record's story list confirms. He is a narrative animal, not a ceremonial spirit; the 'spirit' type is a template label.

description: Black Hactcin is the most powerful of the Hactcin holy beings in Jicarilla Apache creation tradition. He shaped the first four-legged animal from clay and made other animals from parts of its body, then created the first man from turquoise, coral, opal, jet, and abalone brought by the animals. He is a primordial maker and protector.
source: Jicarilla Apache creation account (Goddard 1911; Opler); input appearance verified
research_notes: Tribe: Jicarilla Apache. Black Hactcin is the most powerful Hactcin; he created the first four-legged animal from clay and the first man from precious stones (input's appearance text is accurate and verified). He is a primordial maker rather than a nature-spirit.

description: In Ruth Benedict's version of the Zuni emergence, the people lived in darkness in the fourth world and recognized Awonawilona's two sons, the twin war gods, as their bow priests. The bow priests led the people upward, planting prayer sticks that grew into ladders, and shaped human bodies, cutting mouths, fingers, and toes and removing horns and tails.
source: Benedict 1935, Zuni Mythology; Wikipedia, Zuni mythology
research_notes: Tribe: Zuni. In Benedict's version, Awonawilona's two sons (the twin war gods) are recognized by the people as 'their bow priests' and lead the emergence, planting prayer sticks that grow into ladders and shaping human bodies. Verified against Wikipedia's Zuni mythology article.

description: In the Zuni kachina-origin tradition, the Beloved Twins led the three groups of Zuni during the clan migrations in search of the middle place, itiwana. Under their guidance the clans separated by direction, and their journeys are recalled in Zuni origin narratives. They are migration leaders of the emerging people.
source: Cushing 1896; Wikipedia, Zuni mythology (kachina tradition)
research_notes: Tribe: Zuni. The Beloved Twins led the three Zuni groups during the clan migration in search of itiwana, the middle place (Wikipedia's Zuni mythology account of the kachina tradition, following Cushing). Distinct from the Ahayu'da twin war gods.

description: Bohpoli, meaning the Thrower, also called Kowi Anukasha, the Forest Dweller, are little people of the Choctaw who live alone in the thick, dark woods. About two feet tall, they throw sticks at travelers and are mischievous, yet they are said to share medicine knowledge with those who treat the woods with respect. Documented by Swanton.
source: Swanton 1931; Native-Languages.org, Kowi Anukasha
research_notes: Tribe: Choctaw. Bohpoli ('the Thrower') and Kowi Anukasha ('Forest Dweller') are attested little people of the Choctaw, documented by John Swanton; see also native-languages.org. The input's summary and fun fact are accurate and were condensed.
